Checkpoints don't require this storage, since they are identifiable by height alone (once headers have been validated, which precedes any storage). This allows that to be performed concurrently, which is a material savings depending on platform. For checkpoints these records are logically irreversible. Checkpoints don't require this storage, since they are identifiable by height alone (once headers have been validated, which precedes any storage). Consequently it is the case that a milestone block may end up in a branch that does not actually contain the configured milestone (though must have at one point). In other words, a block that is valid under milestone necessarily remains valid in any other context. This observation simplifies the reorg of a milestone branch, since blocks below the fork point are unaffected by the reorg (i.e. do not have to be validated).

elements.text: The final step is confirmation (as opposed to confirmability checks).
strong_tx
is associated for a block
before
the confirmability checks for that block occur. This allows the block to be identified as part of the candidate chain under check without identifying the candidate blocks above it as so. But
confirmation

is the process of reorganizing a confirmable candidate chain into the confirmed height index. Not until that point is any block in the candidate chain considered confirmed (despite being and "strong" and "confirmable"). Confirmable (unlike the strong association) is a terminal state. So a confirmable block never needs to be revalidated (i.e. for reorganization). The final step of confirmation is not necessary (or even used) for validating subsequent blocks, as that is all performed in the candidate chain, and organizing an entire 850k blocks as confirmed (
push_confirmed
) under milestone takes only a couple seconds.

I think this will be resolved through locality. During initial and catch-up sync, organization starts once there is a stronger candidate chain, and that evaluation (download/validation/confirmability) starts once there is a current header chain. This results in a cascade of single block organizations, since the next block in order is always a stronger chain than that previously confirmed.

Consequently with concurrent validation/confirmation the same inputs/outputs/prevouts and indexes will already be paged in as a consequence of full block and prevout population. This makes navigating the links for confirmability almost free and should preclude paging. The only additional searches, reads and writes are to the strong_tx table, however this is a small table (tx scale with little data) that should not cause thrashing.

So instead of running confirmation in series it makes a lot more sense to run it concurrently, and instead to run download and validation/confirmability in series.

I updated the confirmation chaser to use a single thread high priority pool to chase validations and dispatch confirmability checks. [This caused me to notice that the validation chaser should also use an independent thread (not just independent strand on the network threadpool) for monitor and dispatch of validation jobs, either in high or normal priority as configured.] Confirmability still uses c++17 std::transform in the database query, which will project the three subqueries onto all available threads, on current thread priority.

This will cause confirmation to stay close with validation (configured presently for normal thread priority). It will fall behind as it waits on validation gaps, which could be as high as the download window size (currently 50k blocks) but will catch up as gaps are filled. And of course excess CPU capacity will continue to fill in from the validator and downloader. Ideally we would want highest priority on confirm, lower on validate, and lower on download... but we really don't want to be below normal thread priority for any.

elements.text: For one, since there is no utxo set, prevouts are verified unspent by looking up the outpoint’s spending transaction and verifying that it does not exist. This to me would seem slower than looking up the prevout from a utxo set.

Yes, verifying prior existence and unspentness in the strong chain is more expensive for a number of reasons, though the size of the index isn't really one of them. Indexation performance is almost entirely a function of rate of hash collisions, and that is controllable via config. It is also affected by the amount of RAM, and with sufficient RAM the entire store and all indexes are memory resident.

One of the reasons it's slower is that the data model is relational, so there are a large number of queries involved in comping to resolution of this question. Another is that we store conflicting txs and unconfirmed txs in the same tables. However these are tradeoffs. Rapid response to these two questions is not the measure of performance during catchup, compact notification, or otherwise.

The time where it would be considered most critical might be during compact block notification for a miner. We operate under the assumption (as does the usefulness of the protocol itself) that in this scenario we have already seen most if not all txs in the block, apart from the coinbase. In that ideal case libbitcoin has already validated, stored, and indexed all but one tx, which itself does not spend. These txs are not revalidated (unless there is a context incompatibility from the time of pooling, which would be very rare), moved or modified in any way upon possible confirmation. We also don't construct or serialize a block.

We store/index only the header and coinbase, under PoW protection, and then ensure that the block is valid and confirmable via navigation of the tx graph. Unless there is a miss in the pool (which may require a store lookup or peer query) the question of validity can be answered without querying the store. Similarly block templates can be generated from the pool without hitting the store. The graph does not store txs, and for a miner it would be entirely reasonable to have every confirmable (including conflicts) tx ever seen represented in the graph in RAM.

Based on insights from a private conversation, Libbitcoin will also skip checking confirmability if below the milestone. This means that transactions are written in order in the confirmability thread, but their inputs are assumed to exist and be yet unspent. Skipping this check is where the real speedup lies I believe, and was not clear to me on first read.
With that in mind, this approach seems more like a combination of assumevalid and assumeutxo, since the signature checks are skipped and the utxo set is assumed to be valid based on the block height.
Transactions are not written in order. Inputs are never assumed to exist or to be unspent (adherence to the milestone
proves
that prevouts exist and are unspent). Under milestone, the performance advantage comes from extreme concurrency. We can and do download the
entire chain

concurrently, though we generally configure to break it up into 50k block chunks which complete before moving to the next. This chunking improves data locality (query perf) and ensures we don't get block 1 last (which significantly delays validation in the concurrent validation scenario). Block height is not the criteria for a milestone (he may just be speaking loosely). The "utxo set" is
proven

to be valid under the assumption of the milestone (i.e. that the milestone represents a valid branch).

So there is no difference whatsoever in the security model of a milestone and assume valid. In fact I formerly assumed theirs worked the way ours does. But now I can see that the architecture doesn't really lend itself to these optimizations. Skipping block validation checks doesn't amount for any of the performance difference, which is visible from the fact that we are unaffected by the lack of SHANI until we become CPU bound.

Skipping the confirmability checks during download (and validation) is a significant performance advantage, as it is what allows parallelism. However, we can fully download, validate, check confirmability, and confirm the entire chain in 6.2 hours on a machine that takes BC over 24 hours (see above). So it is really not the case that skipping these checks during a milestone run is the basis of the performance advantage. We just don't perform unnecessary checks. The true performance advantage comes from massive parallelsism.

elements.text: When a Libbitcoin node serves a block to a peer, it must reconstruct the block into its serialised representation, which will require some compute for each block request. Bitcoin Core, however, stores the blocks on disk in their serialised format and will simply read the block from disk and send it to the peer

This is true, however block responsiveness to peer is not a priority (and such thread priority can be lower than incoming information for example). Download by peers (catch up sync) is a function of concurrency and peer management, not individual node query response. However, given that all recently-accessed portions of the store are memory-resident, and in fact the entire store can be memory resident, this cost can be largely eliminated.

On a $350 32GB machine libbitcoin can store and index 850,000 blocks in 50 minutes (network limited). This includes tx hashing (twice for witness txs) and Merkle root (twice for witness blocks) for the entire chain, without even having AVX512 or SHANI. When blocks are deserialized there is no hashing at all. So store query performance doesn't appear to be a material issue.

elements.text:
The operating principle of load balancing between the phases is that the downloader would race ahead of the validator if the validator was not higher priority. But as such the validator takes over cycles from the downloader until the validator is starved for work. The confirmer is much faster than the validator, but must wait on validator completions and is totally block ordered. So the confirmer is given a higher priority than the validator. This ensures that confirmations will not get too far behind the validator. Typically (but not strongly) the difference between downloader and confirmer will be no more than the arbitrary download concurrency window (default 50k blocks).

This has the very significant advantage of maximizing data locality, as download->validate->confirm are all operating over the same data. When the required data is is RAM it's practically free in relation to SSD retrieval. This is in large part due to mmap paging and the possibility of getting into a thrashing scenario - where read or write and flush are taking up most of the cycles instead of a tiny portion.

This was a resounding success, not only in the material reduction to the big box run (.5-1.0 hrs out of 6) but also in the mini run.

The mini currently has a validation completion rate of almost 12 hours (plus 1 hours download). This is significantly increased by lack of SHANI, since validation is entirely CPU bound. On the same box, with SHANI implemented, BC takes 15 hours. On a much bigger box without SHANI, Core takes 24 hours - almost doubling the cost. We also have the old libsecp256k1 affecting us here. And our AVX512 implementation doesn't help us because the box doesn't have it. In other words, despite all of that libbitcoin is still about an hour faster than BC if you don't consider confirmation. We should expect BN validation time on mini to be dramatically reduced, possibly in half, to around 6 hours, in an apples-to-apples to BC. On the big box (which is apples-to-apples) BC takes 24.5 hours and BN takes 6.2 (both full validation/confirmation).

But confirmation has been the big issue on the mini, due to thrashing from restricted RAM. However, by running confirmation concurrently with and in proximity to validation, the paging cost is dramatically reduced, basically everything is disk-read once instead of twice. So taking advantage of mmap page locality reduced a full run from ~47 to 18 hours. Considering the lack of SHANI alone, and with no other improvements, this will already outperform BC on the mini. I saw that earlier, and made some comments on it here.

The first observation is that serving up blocks to peers is not a performance critical operation, either for the node or its peers.

Secondly, BN reads, parses, and serializes the entire chain (and does everything else for a milestone run, which is a lot, including all the hashing - not required on read) in about 50 minutes, and would be closer to 40 minutes with sufficient RAM, on a network connection that produces a theoretical limit of 38 minutes to transfer the entire chain as a single file. Reading should therefore be much faster than the network can handle.

Thirdly, there are a number of significant advantages in getting to completion with a compact block. There's no reason to assume that the means of verifying confirmability will have a greater cost than a utxo model, or that the other material advantages won't be dominant (for example, BN does not have to create or serialize a block).

elements.text: There are of course tradeoffs. Concurrency imposes synchronization cost, which has to be measured against the benefit. For example, it is not required that txs be validated with their block, and it is not required that all previous blocks (or txs) be downloaded in order to validate a given block's txs. However tracking and notifying a tx (or block) that all of its required previous outputs have been downloaded is more costly than the partial ordering by block constraint.

elements.text: The download window purposely does not constrain either the validator or the confirmer, and the validator does not constraint the confirmer. However with all having work, naively the highest priority threads should generally exhaust first. But this makes certain assumptions about thread scheduling. The proactor work queues are managed by BOOST ASIO. There is the network pool (download and eventing), validator queue (validation dispatch and validation), and the confirmation queue. c++ is performing the confirmability fan-out (internal to each block), and is starting from the highest priority single thread. Once that thread loops through all blocks, fanning out for each, ASIO takes over to notify it again. And there are almost always confirmation messages in this stranded (ordered) queue. But I suspect that this one highest priority thread is not able to keep pace with 64 high priority validation threads (and 16 normal priority download threads).

elements.text: Finally, as a reminder, this run is on a machine without AVX512 (which is very common for the last five years or so, and we have implemented) and BN doesn't yet apply SHANI (also common on hardware). with these applied it should significantly reduce archive and validation time, which leaves more time for confirmation. elements.text:
This mini run lacks SHANI, so the most comparable runs with BC would be the maxi validation run on Windows 10 (256GB RAM/64 threads, no SHANI), which completes in 24.6 hours. Also the BC macOS (768GB RAM/32 threads, no SHANI) NON-validation run, which completes in 18 hours (I would estimate this would be at least 24 hours with full validation based on lower core speed and lack of SHANI).

So the milestone comparison of BN to BC on the mini is 1.0 hours to 14.1 hours (BN=7%BC), and the comparable (no-SHANI) full validation run (on the Win10 maxi) is 5.6 hours  to 24.6 hours (BN=23%BC).

However, it's not clear that BN can achieve comparable full validation performance on the mini due to the (straightforward) SHANI/SECP256 upgrades. It may be that BN becomes RAM/SSD bound by confirmation before those updates can provide a significant advantage (on higher RAM machines this cost goes away entirely).

Basically the confirmation cost is quadratic in the size of RAM, starting from zero cost at "full" RAM and increasing quadratically as RAM decreases. With full RAM BN becomes fully CPU bound in validation/confirmation like BC. But BC doesn't scale with more RAM, so this low end machine advantage will continue to decrease as RAM cost drops.

I'm not aware of anything significant that BC can do to become scalable, short of a complete rearchitecture. I'm also not aware of anything that BN can do to overcome quadratic validation cost on low RAM machines. However, with milestone sync (default) BN enjoys an order of magnitude advantage on low end machines.

text: This approach also allows us to vectorize K additions, because they are applied across the fully scheduled buffer. In the typical `shani` algorithm (using rotating variables as opposed to a message buffer), this vectorization is limited to 4 lanes (4 concurrent additions). This is however independent of the actual `shani` implementation. By separating the implementation in this manner we can take advantage of 4/8/16 lane vectorization for K additions - mixing `avx512` and `shani`.
